THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

People preserved in cold landscapes

Cold can preserve clothing, hair, food residues and skin, but the circumstances differ from place to place. Some people died while travelling and were recovered from ice or meltwater. Others were buried by their communities and preserved in dry graves or frozen chambers. The histories of who studied, cared for and returned these people differ as much as their preservation.

Selected northern cases from the Alps, Greenland, northwestern North America and the Altai. The companion Andean guide treats high-elevation Inca offerings separately.

Landscape and objects

The whole area in view

Wide northern comparison across modern continents. Pins distinguish regional recovery localities, settlement anchors and modern collections. The Tatshenshini-Alsek point represents the park region.

  1. Tisenjoch / Giogo di Tisa, Alps

    3350–3120 cal BCE, found 1991

    Snow, ice and a sheltered depression preserved a Copper Age man’s body and belongings. [1] [2] [3]

    46.78°, 10.84°

  2. Theodul Pass, Swiss–Italian Alps

    Around 1600 CE, modern recoveries

    Coins and other belongings identify the period of an early modern traveller recovered from the glacier area. His occupation is uncertain. [4] [5]

    45.94°, 7.71°

  3. Qilakitsoq near Uummannaq, Greenland

    Burial about 1475 CE, found 1972

    Two graves held six Inuit women and two boys. Cold, dry conditions helped preserve bodies and garments in a sheltered setting. [6] [7]

    70.67°, -52.13°

  4. Nuuk, Greenland

    Modern museum reference

    The Greenland National Museum and Archives is the museum reference for the Qilakitsormiut display, distinct from the burial locality. [6]

    64.18°, -51.73°

  5. Tatshenshini-Alsek Park region, British Columbia

    About 1670–1850 cal CE, found 1999

    Kwäday Dän Ts’ìnchi’s glacier recovery took place within this broader park landscape. The anchor identifies a region rather than the recovery location. [8] [9] [10]

    59.70°, -137.40°

  6. Pazyryk cemetery region, Altai

    Iron Age, second half of first millennium BCE

    At Pazyryk, ice formed within several burial mounds and preserved otherwise fragile burial materials and human remains. [11] [12]

    50.74°, 88.06°

  7. Ukok Plateau area, southern Altai

    Iron Age, found in 1993

    An ice-filled chamber on the Ukok Plateau held a woman buried among objects and materials preserved in the cold. The plateau point gives regional context. [13] [14] [15]

    49.32°, 87.65°

  8. Anokhin National Museum, Gorno-Altaisk

    Return to the Altai Republic in 2012

    The woman from Ak-Alakha-3 was returned to the Altai Republic after research in Novosibirsk. The modern museum is mapped separately. [15]

    51.96°, 85.95°

Three preservation settings

In a glacier or ice patch, cold can slow decay and help preserve material exposed again by melting. In a sheltered grave, cold and dry air can contribute to dehydration. At Pazyryk, ice developed inside burial chambers and preserved deposits assembled through burial rites. These processes sometimes act together, and surviving material can deteriorate quickly after exposure. Archaeologists ask how a body reached its setting, where cold acted, and which materials later moved. [3] [6] [12] [8]

Ötzi and the Tisenjoch hollow

Ötzi died in the late fourth millennium BCE. Hikers found him in 1991 near the Austria–Italy border. A shallow hollow and changing snow and ice protected many of his belongings. Research continues into whether the find underwent repeated episodes of melt, exposure and displacement. It is possible to read the arrow wound and compare the materials in his toolkit even when the precise way the body reached the hollow is unresolved. [1] [2] [3]

A traveller of another Alpine age

Coins, shoes, arms and equipment from the Theodul glacier in Switzerland point to an early modern traveller, with the coins supporting a date around 1600. This was a different period of travel and trade across the Alps, and the assemblage speaks through objects with a different material history. The familiar label “mercenary” is a historical nickname. The traveller’s occupation remains uncertain and the objects’ movements in the ice make their original arrangement difficult to reconstruct. [4] [5]

A community burial near Uummannaq

At Qilakitsoq, two graves held six women and two boys buried in skins and clothing. Greenland’s National Museum and Archives dates the burial group to around 1475 and discusses family relationships spanning the two graves. Hans and Jokum Grønvold found them in 1972. Dry and cold conditions in the sheltered graves preserved several of the people. The death of all eight has no established single explanation. The burial grouping describes how they were cared for after death. [6] [7] [16]

Garments, skin and change after recovery

Inuit seamstresses selected and worked animal skins into garments suited to Arctic conditions. The graves preserved details of seams, layering and how garments fit together. The evidence also includes amulets and skin markings. Conservation investigations after recovery addressed damage from fungi, an illustration of how organisms and humidity can become problems under new conditions. Each current display and research collection has a different history from the people’s original clothing and burial. [6] [17] [18]

A person found in Champagne and Aishihik territory

In 1999, hunters encountered frozen remains in the Tatshenshini-Alsek region. Champagne and Aishihik First Nations led work concerning the person they named Kwäday Dän Ts’ìnchi, often translated as Long Ago Person Found. Radiocarbon modelling that combined bone collagen with a robe put the man between about 1670 and 1850 calibrated CE. Earlier dates on associated objects had suggested a different age. Marine foods affect radiocarbon interpretation, and objects that appear together after melting can have entered the landscape at different times. [19] [10] [8] [9]

What food sources say about travel

Bone chemistry indicates substantial marine food in his longer-term diet, even though the glacier was well inland. Evidence from plants and animals recovered in the investigation helps connect parts of his recent experience with coast and mountain environments. Marine isotope signatures can reflect food transferred through trade or carried on a journey. They are one component of a reconstruction that includes material evidence and Indigenous knowledge of travel through the region. [8] [20] [19]

Family connections and responsibility

The Champagne and Aishihik First Nations community DNA study reported 17 relatives from Yukon and Alaska. The project’s public records discuss the family finding, community events and knowledge about the land. The biological evidence can support recognition of a maternal relationship. Contemporary kinship, care, knowledge and authority also come from the community, which set priorities for work on the find and directed commemoration and return. [21] [22] [19]

Burial ice at Pazyryk

Altai burial mounds contained wooden chambers and carefully assembled grave deposits. In several mounds water froze within or around the chambers and ice protected felt, leather, wood, textiles and the remains of people and horses. Some human bodies had also undergone deliberate funeral preparation. Post-burial freezing and cultural preparation each contributed to what survived, alongside disturbance and excavation. The distribution is uneven even within one cemetery. [11] [12] [14]

Ukok and the debates about care

The individual from Ak-Alakha-3 on the Ukok Plateau is connected to the broader Pazyryk archaeological tradition, in a different burial and landscape from the Pazyryk cemetery. Following research in Novosibirsk, her body returned to the Anokhin National Museum in Gorno-Altaisk in 2012. Ethnographic research describes disputes about display, return and ways of caring for her. Many Indigenous Altai people opposed public display. A regional guide can teach about the burial through its landscape, documented material context and the positions expressed by people with relationships to it. [13] [15] [14]

What an image can reveal or expose

Near-infrared recording of a tattooed woman from Pazyryk Barrow 5 clarified darkened designs and showed differences in the way parts of the tattoos were made. The work addresses marks on a particular individual, with technique inferred from detail rather than observing the act itself. Research images provide evidence in a scientific setting, while whether and how to show people’s remains publicly remains a question of care and community authority. The map uses landscapes and place descriptions to support comparison. [23] [24] [15]

How the cases differ

Person or groupPreservation contextBasis for dating and interpretationSources
ÖtziA high Alpine hollow influenced by ice, snow and meltwater.Direct calibrated radiocarbon range. Subsequent movement and exposure are under study.[2] [3]
Theodul travellerGlacier finds from an Alpine crossing, including fragments of human remains and possessions.Coins date the assemblage to around 1600. The traveller’s occupation remains uncertain.[4] [5]
QilakitsormiutDeliberate Inuit burials, with cold and drying in a sheltered setting.Burial context, radiocarbon and textile studies. Cause of death unresolved.[6] [7] [17]
Kwäday Dän Ts’ìnchiGlacier recovery in community territory, with clothing and other objects.Combined robe and bone dates, with attention to marine diet and possible multiple episodes of site use.[19] [8]
Pazyryk and UkokNatural ice in chambers prepared for burial, at distinct localities.Archaeology, wood and associated artefacts. Dating and mortuary practice vary by mound.[11] [12] [13]
